items.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: And I played with Marian McPartland and she liked me and hired me and that kind of got me started

ctx.x: When you look at the Local 802 union book, you see an awful lot of players. And what was it like, trying to find a niche?

My wife at the time had a job in New York so it took the financial pressure off, which I think that’s the main thing. New York — in that time there was a lot more work in the town, in ‘68, but it was very frightening to me, so again I was still very insecure and I was not the kind of guy to go out and sit in in clubs and say here I am, which I’ve known in subsequent years, guys that had that kind of moxie, and I admire that, but I had a few contacts from Woody’s band and I think I played with John Bunch…
There’s some nice quotes in a Jazz Times article that just came out, about her. Have you seen it yet?

items.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997
items.q: because I had Michael Moore with me, who was very much into, like he wrote several of those tunes

ctx.x: Very, quite free. and I was wondering if this is how you went into this record, and said we’re really going to — I don’t know what phrase to use — push the envelope here.

No, I think I was pretty much doing that kind of thing because I had Michael Moore with me, who was very much into, like he wrote several of those tunes. It’s funny, after a while Michael Moore became very conservative and I always felt bad because it seemed like he led me into this and every time somebody’s around that it’s going to be a little free – I’ll fall back in. I mean I can’t really do it by myself. I’m trying to think exactly when it happened. I think I was playing a place called The Apartment, it was…

made “Ambiance” anyway, and before I had Michael Moore. And this drummer named Jimmy Cappers kept saying, “why don’t you play free — why don’t you play free things?” And I really couldn’t sort of quite understand what it was I had to do, and I kept trying and I’d always end up in a triad or something. And finally I was able to do that very thing. I mean I can do it. But at that time I probably never would have thought of doing “Piano Jazz” with Cecil Taylor. But it’s funny now I love doing that. But I don’t know…

items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think I took my own trio at that time. I think I took Michael Moore

ctx.x: I didn’t know him at that period of course. And Alan may have been out with Lionel Hampton at that particular time, so that may have . . .

I don’t know. I didn’t meet Alan until much later, years later. I would go up to Boston. Played at the Jazz Workshop. I think I took my own trio at that time. I think I took Michael Moore, but then I . . . later I did play with Alan at a place called the Stardust Room, which was . . .
